The House of Representatives blocked the impeachment of Pete Hegseth, the Secretary of Defence, on Tuesday 10 November. According to CBS News, the vote was procedural: the House approved by 211 votes to 204 the referral of the eight articles to the Judiciary Committee, which effectively shelves them. Thomas Massie, the Republican representative from Kentucky who had introduced them, was the only Republican to vote with all Democrats against the referral. According to CBS, seven Republicans and 11 Democrats were absent.

The articles accused Hegseth above all of conducting the war against Iran without congressional authorisation. Others concerned the Iranian school that was hit, attacks on small boats in the Caribbean, the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, and the investigations into Senator Mark Kelly. Massie said he was disappointed but not surprised. He added that he will not introduce another impeachment resolution and that he wants to force a vote on a war powers resolution. Massie will leave Congress in January, having lost his primary.

Hegseth called the move a «farce» and political theatre, maintaining that the accusations are disagreements over defence policies and not high crimes. Donald Trump, the president, wrote that the attempt had «failed miserably», CBS reports. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House, said the matter is not closed and that this is only the beginning: Democrats could reintroduce it when they have a majority in both chambers in January.

The Council of Ministers approved the second decree on utility bills on 9 November, which introduces a price cap on gas for thermoelectric power plants, reports Ansa. The Minister of the Environment and Energy Security, Pichetto Fratin, estimates an average cut of about 15 euros per megawatt-hour starting from January 2027, for 18 months. The decree amends Article 6 of the one approved in February.

According to Pichetto, the measure reduces the final price of energy by 4-5% and mobilises more than 3 billion, writes Ansa. For an average family, which consumes about two megawatt-hours a year, the minister estimates a saving of about 30 euros. Codacons, based on those figures, calculates between 27 and 37 euros per year, with the risk that uncertainties could halve the benefits, reports Ansa. Open writes that the actual saving for families is about 20 euros per year. The think tank Ecco calculates 17 euros per year, 1.4 euros per month.

For businesses, the data released after the Council of Ministers indicate about 280 euros for a small artisan business that consumes 40 megawatt-hours a year, about 210,000 euros for a large food company with 30,000 megawatt-hours, and about 520,000 euros for an energy-intensive company with self-production. Meloni said that in the immediate term, the effects for families will be more limited. Angelo Bonelli, of the Green and Left Alliance, argues that the measures are temporary and do not address the structural problem of energy costs.
